attributes.experience:
Eryx is a worker-owned labor cooperative with almost 15 years of experience solving complex problems involving mathematics and software. We are a group of nerdy PhDs with a solid background in math and computer science. Our team has extensive experience in blockchain development, cryptography, and privacy-focused protocols, which gives us the expertise required to successfully deliver the project.
Among other things, we’ve been core contributors to the Lambdaworks library and implemented the CircleSTARKS protocol in GPU alongside with Nethermind. This involved implementing several ZK cryptographic primitives (field operations, polynomial commitment schemes, FRI protocols, FFTs), in different platforms and languages. Furthermore, we implemented a proving system based on the Plonk protocol. During this project we wrote a simple interface to design circuits. It included basic operations and conditionals that made the building blocks for more complex cryptographic primitives. We also developed a Plonky2 backend for Aztec's Noir, funded by the Ethereum Foundation. 
In relation to this proposal, we have extensive experience in Aiken smart contract development, including previously funded proposals under Project Catalyst focused on educational and technical infrastructure for Cardano. We also wrote zk circuits for cryptographic primitives such as hash functions and elliptic curve operations.
We are active contributors to the ENCOINS protocol, currently deployed on the Cardano mainnet with privacy-preserving features. Currently, we are researching the integration of ZK systems with the EUTxO model.

Additionally, the team will seek further support from Catalyst, Intersect technical funding streams, and other grant/funding models to continue iterative development.
attributes.proposal_description:
Our proposal is building a ZK bridge for Cardano, which we will deploy on the Cardano testnet.
As part of this initiative, we will define a communication protocol for the bridge, provide the full source code of the smart contracts on the Cardano side, and produce comprehensive technical documentation detailing the protocol between Cardano and any other isomorphic blockchain. 
We will provide a circuit that enables a relayer to generate the ZK proof that a locking transaction was successfully added to the chain, which can then be verified on the receiving blockchain. This way, any blockchain will be able to implement a ZK bridge with Cardano, leveraging its newly added capability to generate such proofs. This allows for a variety of uses, such as moving assets outside Cardano just by providing the proof that they’ve locked an equivalent amount in the Cardano Smart Contract. The resulting bridge can serve as a generic framework for interoperability between Cardano and any other blockchain willing to implement the corresponding counterpart contracts.
Furthermore, we will implement contracts in Aiken to mint assets on a Cardano-like (isomorphic) blockchain and deploy them on the Cardano testnet, providing a fully functional proof of concept. These building blocks will enable developers to create bridges between Cardano and other chains with minimal additional effort.
attributes.key_proposal_deliverables:
1. Documentation of the communication protocol 
2. Bridge smart contracts in Aiken for locking funds in the Cardano side
3. Bridge smart contracts in Aiken for minting wrapped assets, mocking the ZK proof verification
4. ZK proof that a block containing a locking transaction was added to Cardano
5. Bridge smart contract in Aiken for verifying the ZK proof

attributes.problem_statement:
Cross-chain interoperability remains one of the most critical yet unresolved challenges for Cardano. While the ecosystem is advancing in scalability through projects like Hydra and optimistic roll ups such as Midgard it still lacks a secure, trustless, and modular zk-based bridges infrastructure.
Current bridges rely on centralized validators or multi-signature schemes, introducing major security risks—as demonstrated by numerous high-profile exploits in other ecosystems. Without a native zero-knowledge bridge, Cardano is unable to safely connect with external chains, severely limiting access to external liquidity, composability with other ecosystems, and the ability to scale horizontally.

Furthermore, the Cardano ecosystem lacks a unified open-source toolkit for:
On-chain verification of zero-knowledge proofs
Secure and efficient cross-chain messaging
Asset wrapping and unwrapping under Cardano’s native token model
And trust-minimized interoperability with existing ZK-rollups.

This absence puts Cardano at a competitive disadvantage compared to platforms like Ethereum, which already benefit from multiple zk-based Layer 2 solutions and zk-enabled bridges.
A modular zkBridge is not only critical to unlock interoperability—it also lays the groundwork for a future Cardano-native zkRollup framework, by enabling the testing and deployment of foundational components such as provers, verifiers, and state synchronization mechanisms.
attributes.proposal_benefit:
Building a zero-knowledge bridge provides several key benefits to the Cardano ecosystem. A bridge between Cardano and other blockchains would make it much easier for value to flow in from external ecosystems, increasing the liquidity available within Cardano.
A zero-knowledge bridge, specifically, offers important advantages over alternative architectures such as optimistic bridges. In a ZK bridge, a single user action accompanied by a succinct proof of deposit is sufficient to release tokens on the destination blockchain. This eliminates the need for community-wide monitoring or challenge periods, significantly reducing latency and trust assumptions.
Additionally, by building a ZK bridge, Cardano positions itself as a more interoperable platform, capable of engaging with the broader ecosystem of zero-knowledge technologies. This lays the groundwork for future innovations in identity, privacy-preserving applications, and cross-chain collaboration.
attributes.supplementary_endorsement: The need for ZK solutions in Cardano has been increasingly voiced by the community across multiple forums. There is strong interest in the Cardano ecosystem to support a ZkBridge framework.

attributes.comment_text: Are there any Cardano Budget proposals whose scope may currently overlap with this proposal (especially TSC)?

I would vote no at this time but wanted to give the reasoning. This primarily benefits Cardano at L2, which I think will eventually be needed but in terms of timing that's an area that needs further growth/development before a need like this is really warranted. Maybe my perspective is wrong on that, but just seems a little bit cart before the horse. Ultimately, not confident that Cardano L2 is ready for this yet, at least for the 2025 budget. I have no issues with the total cost, and I will need to personall look into anything that may overlap this.

Hey!! I haven't seen any proposals whose scope currently overlaps with this one. Bridge infrastructure and ZK development are critical areas for Cardano, and aside from this proposal and the zkRollup by ZkFold, no one else seems to be actively working on ZK-related solutions.
We are in contact with members of the TSC, particularly Ben Hart, and we have suggested several areas where Cardano could improve or eventually address ZK-related challenges through the TSC. However, this proposal does not overlap with anything currently included in their scope, nor with the proposal submitted by Input Output.

Hey! Just a quick clarification: while it's true that zk-based bridges can support future L2 expansion, their utility goes far beyond that. These bridges also enable Cardano to connect with other ecosystems such as Bitcoin or Ethereum. This is critical for bringing assets — like stablecoins or BTC — directly onto Cardano's Layer 1, which significantly boosts liquidity on the base layer.

The bridge infrastructure can benefit Cardano L1 by enabling cross-chain capital flow and composability with the broader crypto ecosystem.

Happy to provide more technical detail if helpful — and again, appreciate the thoughtful engagement!

1. Is there any overlap in scope with other proposals related to the Technical Steering Committee (TSC), such as other L2, zk, or bridge initiatives?

2. How is the scope of this proposal differentiated from other zk-related or rollup proposals like Midgard, Tweag’s L2 tooling, or zkFold?

3. Is the budget of 700,000 ADA reasonable for a proposal that aims to deliver a proof-of-concept and not a fully deployed mainnet solution?

4. The deliverables include “mocking the ZK proof verification”—how close is this to actual zk verification, and will it be upgradeable to production-level use?

5. Given that the deployment is limited to the testnet, is there a clear roadmap or criteria for transitioning to mainnet implementation?

6. What guarantees or mechanisms are in place to maintain the bridge and continue development beyond this initial 8-month funding period?

7. While the code will be open-sourced on GitHub, will any security audits or formal verifications be conducted before real-world adoption?

8. How does the team’s involvement in the ENCOINS protocol directly support or validate their capacity to deliver a ZK bridge?

9. Once this proposal is complete, how much additional time and budget do you expect it will take to deploy the mainnet? How much additional treasury withdrawal will be required?
Sorry, I didn't notice agus' message 🙏
Thank you sorry, I didn't notice your message 🙏

Hi Yuta!

1. Answered by Agustin in a previous comment :)

2. Midgard is a Layer 2 solution, but it does not incorporate ZK; rather, it is an optimistic rollup. We did not see anything in Tweag's proposal that includes ZK or any Layer 2 solutions. On the other hand, we differ from ZkFold in the language that we use, since we’re working in Aiken.
Beyond this, the main difference between our proposal and the ones mentioned is that they aim to provide Layer 2 solutions for Cardano, while our bridge proposal offers a solution to connect Cardano with other blockchains in a decentralized and trustless manner. Both contribute to addressing Cardano's scalability and liquidity challenges, but they are complementary approaches.

3. This process has many steps. There are some core functionalities that our proposal will solve, which are building blocks for a testnet AND a mainnet bridge. In particular, the smart contracts, the protocol description and most importantly the Zero Knowledge proof generation for the relayer are modules in the whole system that also solve the problems in mainnet.

We decided not to go for the mainnet yet because we think it’s responsible to break down our processes into smaller iterations, where each incremental step adds value and has a lower uncertainty. For example, getting into transferring real money would require strong legal advice that is not part of the proposal’s budget. Another example is getting a security audit for the ZK circuit. 

Reducing the uncertainty would mean a follow-up proposal to further develop this solution is easier to conceive for both the developers proposing it and the voters considering it.

We think the proposed budget is aligned with other similar proposals, or even a bit lower in terms of expected USD.



The other answers will be in new comments because of the length limit.

4. The ZK proof generation is the main challenge of this proposal and it will take some months until our ZK team can finish it. We will be able to start working on the proof verification after finishing the ZK proof generation (i.e. building the ZK circuit needed to generate the proof). 

Our plan is to have a team working on developing the needed smart contracts, and another team will work in parallel on building the circuit. Since building the contracts will be simpler than making the ZK proof, it’s expected that milestone 2 will be completed before the Zk proof is finished.

The milestone “Bridge smart contracts in Aiken for minting wrapped assets, mocking the ZK proof verification” means building the bridge smart contract for minting without verifying a proof. It is intended for the smart contracts team to be able to keep working on the contracts without being blocked until the Zk team finishes.

TL;DR That milestone is a way for us to organize the workflow. 

5. When we mentioned reducing uncertainty, we meant that we could use this first implementation to complete our understanding of the environment we are working on, and we would be able to use that information to then produce a roadmap detailing what is exactly missing for transitioning to mainnet.

That being said, we are already talking to other developers in the ecosystem to continue this project when it succeeds and also for eventual code audits, for all the different aspects of the proposal.

6. All our contributions will be under a commercial friendly open source license (e.g. Apache 2.0 or MIT), which guarantees that anybody - not only us - can continue development, or even fork & build up on it (for both commercial or non commercial uses).

We think that adapting Cardano to support ZK applications will continue to be in the interest of the community, as it has been until now. This means that many funding opportunities should arise for us and others, to deploy the ZK bridge to mainnet.

We also envision our contributions being employed by players from other ecosystems (blockchains) thanks to the open source licensing chosen, and given that our project will allow them a smoother integration with Cardano.

7. We need an audit for each building block of the bridge before real-world adoption, that’s for sure. We didn’t mention that in the proposal because that’s the next step in the roadmap (and thus it exceeds the current scope). Another thing to notice is that maybe we need different people to conduct each audit depending on the nature of the code. For example, the ZK circuit needs a different treatment than a smart contract in Aiken.

8. We have prior experience working with the Cardano protocol, which is shown in the current proposals that we’re developing (links below). In particular, we’re working on the Proof of Innocence grant alongside the ENCOINS team, to incorporate verifying a Groth16 proof in their application’s workflow.
There are contact points between that use case and ours, because both require to generate a smart contract that, among other things, verifies a (most likely) Groth16 proof. Since the verifier contract is generic, this prior work is relevant for the current project.

I consider "ZK Bridge" to be a very important project and am considering voting yes. So here's my question.
Regarding the "introduction of external liquidity and enhancement of DeFi infrastructure," it states that the implementation of ZK Bridge will make it easier to move funds from other blockchains to Cardano, but what would this look like as a concrete service? For example, would it become possible to transfer Ethereum's ETH or USDT to the Cardano network?

This grant doesn't cover the construction of such service directly, but it creates all the necessary building blocks from the Cardano side. As a bridge must be supported in both of the blockchains involved, the development of a fully functional bridge between them includes contracts in both. With the tools we aim to provide, anyone can, for example, create a bridge between Cardano and Ethereum providing only the contracts in the Ethereum side.
As for the asset transfer question, this problem has a standard solution in the bridging technology. When you transfer using bridges, what's really transferred is a wrapped representation of the original token, which keeps an 1:1 exchange value with the original token of the original network. For example, if you build a bridge with Ethereum, if you lock, say, 10 ETH in the Ethereum side, you get permission to mint 10 native tokens in Cardano, each representing 1 ETH. Typically we would call this new Cardano token WETH, or Wrapped ETH. Anyone can later burn WETH to get permission to unlock ETH in the original contract. In a ZK bridge, the "giving permission to mint" and "to unlock" actions are implemented with ZK proofs.
